title: The oldest tool, about to carry new weight
paras: Let's start with the oldest tool in the box — and the one about to carry real new weight. You draw a line round a town or village: inside, development's acceptable in principle; outside, you're in countryside, where the restraint policies bite. Nearly every rural plan leans on it, under a range of names — development limits, village envelopes, built-up area boundaries — used everywhere, yet never under a common method. It comes from the post-war containment tradition, and most boundaries on today's maps were never drawn under any stated methodology — converted from older designations, amended piecemeal with no recorded criteria, then defended at examination on assertion. Hence the familiar anomalies: lines that cut through gardens, exclude infill plots for no articulable reason, take in land nobody can explain.

For forty years that didn't much matter. The boundary decided which side of the countryside policies a site fell on, and its force rose and fell with the plan's health — up to date and delivering, it held; five-year supply fails or the plan ages, and the tilted balance sweeps it aside. A generation of appeals turned on whether restrictive settlement policies were out of date. Now the draft Framework restructures it: local plans must set a clear spatial strategy — boundaries, or criteria — determining where the presumption in favour of sustainable development applies. Within settlements, proposals are supported unless the harms substantially outweigh the benefits; outside, the presumption applies only to a defined list — under-delivery, certain rural categories. Add national decision-making policies, against which inconsistent local policies carry very limited weight, a thirty-month plan cycle, and the old system closing to submissions at the end of 2026. If the final Framework holds, the boundary stops being a soft policy line and becomes the switch that turns the presumption on or off — and lines of that pedigree are about to carry the weight. Promoters will test the weak ones, objectors the generous ones, inspectors the methodology, where one exists.

title: The legal frame: Braintree and the limits of the line
paras: Now the legal frame, and it's humbling for anyone who treats the line as self-executing. It turns on Braintree: the Court of Appeal held that national policy contains no definition of a settlement or village, sets no minimum number of dwellings, and doesn't require a settlement to be defined by a boundary in any plan. Whether a group of dwellings amounts to a settlement is a matter of fact and judgment, and isolation carries its ordinary meaning — physical separateness from built form. Two things follow. A boundary can't conclusively define what is or isn't a settlement for national policy. And land outside the line isn't automatically isolated countryside — a dwelling beyond it may still be at a settlement as a matter of fact, and the isolated-homes policy isn't engaged just because the map says so.

The plan-making side of the same principle: a settlement boundary isn't a tool for identifying what's part of a village — it identifies a single cohesive built-up area. So outlying dwellings socially part of a settlement, the farmstead that's always belonged, the cottages up the lane, may quite properly fall outside; social and historic membership is one question, physical cohesion another, and the line answers only the second. And the corollary runs through the last decade of appeals: the boundary is only as strong as the plan's delivery. Where supply failed, boundaries got swept aside by the tilted balance — and the draft Framework still applies the presumption outside settlements where supply or delivery fail. The line doesn't defend the plan. The plan defends the line.

title: The common core: criteria that recur
paras: So what's the common core? Strip the terminology and the independent methodologies converge on six recurring elements. First, built form: the boundary defines the built extent, and land comes in where it forms part of that built character — dwellings and curtilages where the curtilage closely relates to the built form and is enclosed, plus community facilities and their curtilages, and employment sites integral to the settlement. Second, character exclusions: land's out where bringing it in would harm the character, structure or form — large gardens, paddocks and orchards, open spaces at the edge, sports fields, allotments. The consolidated list adds isolated development cut off from the settlement, agricultural buildings and farmsteads on the fringe, paddocks into open countryside, open recreational land with little built form, green gaps and local green spaces, and buildings whose use sits more with the countryside.

Third, edge cases resolved by relationship, not proximity: converted agricultural buildings included only where not visually or physically detached, and excluded even when adjacent if they keep a separate character — a separate access, or membership of a larger farm complex. That bites on the growing stock of Class Q conversions at settlement edges, contested parcel by parcel. Fourth, physical features: boundaries follow, but don't include, defined features — walls, hedgerows, roads, tracks, watercourses, field boundaries. The point is durability: a line on a hedge survives; one across an open field invites dispute.

Two disciplines finish it. The commitments cut-off: reviews run against a fixed snapshot date, ignoring mid-review permissions — unimplemented ones out, as not yet built form; commenced ones in, as their layout's certain; stale allocations stripped. And the audit trail: a numbered criteria set, then a settlement-by-settlement schedule recording every change against the criterion that justifies it, with segment-level scoring sheets doing the same stretch by stretch.

title: The five design choices
paras: Beyond the core, five decisions where authorities have gone opposite ways. First: boundaries, or criteria? Cornwall abolished its boundaries for criteria — infill of small gaps in continuous frontage, rounding off, and previously developed land within or immediately adjoining a settlement at an appropriate scale, with express protection for significant gaps. The trade is flexibility — and organic growth across settlements of all sizes — against constant uncertainty over what's a small gap or a rounding-off, fought application by application. Under the draft Framework the two are alternative mechanisms for where the presumption applies — criteria buy flexibility by moving the argument out of the examination into every application.

Second: tight or loose? East Devon drew its existing boundaries tightly to constrain growth, its new ones loosely to yield small sites under a hectare, backing national small-sites policy. Tightness isn't technical, it's a growth-strategy call — and a boundary constraining housing land against strategic policy risks failing the basic conditions. Third, a middle way for small villages: lighter-touch infill boundaries admitting modest development without full within-settlement status, or a policy allowing schemes of fewer than twenty-five dwellings adjoining the line at service villages. Both calibrate how much presumption a small village gets.

Fourth: district or parish? Some districts draw and review boundaries themselves, letting neighbourhood plans adjust through a sufficiently advanced process. Others defer outright where a neighbourhood plan designates them, or delegate infill settlements and their boundaries to neighbourhood plans; and South Oxfordshire defines none at all, the whole exercise handed to its parishes and supported by the only free-standing published guide to the subject. Delegation buys local knowledge and ownership; the price is patchwork coverage, inconsistent criteria between neighbouring parishes, and the cross-parish problem — a boundary crossing a parish line can only be amended on one side. Under the new Framework, unparished or plan-less parts of a delegating district may lack the very boundaries or criteria the presumption depends on.

Fifth: the Green Belt line. Where settlements sit in Green Belt, wash-over or inset is a distinct assessment — each village judged on its open character and contribution to openness, with a recommendation on insetting. Where the settlement boundary is also the Green Belt boundary, moving one moves the other, engaging the exceptional-circumstances regime. And a boundary policy can send everything outside the line to Green Belt policy — one line fixing the reach of two national regimes. Double freight, double care.

title: The ten-step method and the model criteria
paras: Now the method — and the model criteria. The boundary question is logically second; first is the settlement hierarchy. The worked model screened around five hundred and fifty settlements against a threshold — a hundred people, or fifty dwellings — then scored survivors on services, facilities, broadband, employment and public transport, weighting rural multi-function premises as community hubs, and held the methodology constant across three iterations as the data refreshed. The upshot: upper tiers get boundaries, the smallest get none and fall to countryside and exceptions policies — or the hierarchy becomes a matrix parishes drawing their own lines must respect.

Synthesised, it runs to ten steps. Decide the instrument — boundaries, criteria or hybrid — as a recorded strategy call. Decide the tier: who draws, who reviews, what deference neighbourhood boundaries get, how cross-parish settlements are handled. Settle the hierarchy on that thresholded model, fixing method before applying it. Declare the strategy of the line, tight or loose, tied to small-sites and windfall assumptions. Adopt the criteria before drawing. Fix the snapshot date. Draw at the desk, then verify on the ground — mapping and aerial imagery, planning history for every edge site, site visits before publishing. Write the two-limbed policy. Record every line against a criterion in a schedule. And build in the review regime.

Then the model criteria — each tested in consultation somewhere in England. The inclusion and exclusion tests largely restate the core we've walked, so I won't relist every line. What the model adds on inclusion is the commitments: commenced permissions and firm allocations at the snapshot date, with a call on whether allocation green buffers come inside, plus previously developed land within — or, where strategy supports, adjoining — the built-up area. On exclusion it adds unimplemented permissions and stale allocations, and it names coalescence buffers alongside the green gaps and local green spaces. Then the drawing rules: follow but don't include defined physical features; boundaries need not be continuous — distinct clusters can carry more than one line, gaps protected; flag where the line meets a Green Belt boundary; keep to the built-up area, not the social settlement; and record every segment against the criteria.

The policy is two-limbed: what's supported within the boundary — conditioned on character, design codes and the rest of the development plan, never absolute — and what governs outside, tied to countryside, Green Belt or exceptions policies. A boundary without an outside limb is a line without consequences. And the best policies anticipate their failure modes — one made plan withholds support from development inside the boundary that would, individually or cumulatively, extend linear form along a road or watercourse out of keeping with a historic nucleated pattern: an answer to the within-boundary ribbon problem. On presentation, contested segments get layered justification — aerial imagery, historic mapping, annotated features — with clean cartography, distinct line styles, keys, scale, and cross-reference to the criteria.

title: What survives examination — and what falls
paras: Finally — what survives, and what falls. Survives: boundaries adopted through a published, criteria-based methodology with a settlement-by-settlement audit trail, where an inspector can trace any contested line to a stated criterion and a recorded judgment, and defend a segment with its own layered mapping rather than institutional memory. Boundaries aligned with a thresholded hierarchy inherit its evidence. Criteria from the common core are hard to attack, because they recur independently across the country. Two-limbed policies give decision-makers something to apply. And a policy that connects to the growth strategy — why the lines are tight or loose, how the windfall assumptions depend on it — meets the justification question head on.

Falls: inherited lines defended on assertion fall first — no methodology, every anomaly exposed. Then boundaries doing silent policy work: lines drawn tight to suppress growth while the plan claims a positive strategy invite modification — the record includes an inspector rewriting an over-restrictive countryside policy at examination to restore the flexibility national policy expects. At neighbourhood level it's sharper: a boundary constraining housing land against strategic policies can fail the basic conditions and sink the plan. Loosely drafted criteria just relocate the dispute. One-limbed policies, silent on the outside or forgetful of the Green Belt regime, unravel in decision-taking. And above all, out-of-date plans — the last decade of appeals is dominated by boundaries swept aside where supply failed, and the draft Framework carries that straight on.

The inherited-anomaly problem is a failure of review, so the discipline is a review regime. A stated cycle, five years or each plan review. Automatic reassessment when the plan or strategy above changes, and when major committed development completes. Triggers for earlier review — a delivery shortfall, significant demographic or economic change, infrastructure altering a settlement's sustainability, environmental change like revised flood mapping. And firmly: boundary change happens only through plan review, never by concession in a decision.

A candid note to close. The case law is verified; the examination and appeal patterns are stated at pattern level, from harvested documents, made neighbourhood plans and established practice — a counted sample of decisions, and a check against the final Framework, come next. But the opportunity is real: the system is about to hang the presumption on lines most authorities can't currently justify. Every component of a defensible methodology has been tested somewhere in public; what's never existed is the synthesis. Adopt one deliberately, before your lines are tested, and you hold the high ground; understand the methodology, and you know where inherited lines are weakest. And parishes drawing under delegation need the same framework, so the map doesn't fragment.
